title: An array of challenges - and opportunities
abstract:
The future is bright for solar energy. The cost of electricity from photovoltaic solar power has decreased dramatically in recent years, facilitating much of the large-scale solar energy developments we see across the U.S. today. Even more solar energy development is expected to come as we seek economic and carbon-neutral ways to satisfy the country’s growing electricity needs. 
To be on track for net-zero carbon dioxide emissions by the middle of the century, the U.S. would need to generate about 1,000 gigawatts of solar energy by 2035—mostly by ground-based utility-scale solar plants (DOE 2021). That is more than 10 times the current amount of utility-scale solar development (SEIA 2022)—enough to power all U.S. homes. Since photovoltaic power is by far the most common solar energy technology type and is expected to outpace other solar technologies—such as concentrated solar power—this article focuses solely on PV developments.
 A challenge for solar energy, however, is its relatively low power density and poor land-use efficiency. Utility-scale solar energy requires large amounts of land. The typical footprint of a utility-scale PV facility is between 5 and 7.5 acres per megawatt (DOE 2021). Achieving the 2034 solar energy projections could require as much as 7.5 million acres—roughly equivalent to the area of the state of Maryland. 
The increased pressure on land for solar development presents ecological challenges in terms of potential habitat loss and wildlife mortality associated with the construction and infrastructure (Lovich and Ennen 2011; Smallwood 2022). The question before us is, how can we mitigate these impacts and make solar energy development more ecologically compatible?
